title: The Centre Just Cut Ujjwala Subsidised Cylinders from Nine to Four. Ten Crore Households Will Feel It.
excerpt: The government says the average Ujjwala family uses only four refills a year. Critics say that average exists because families cannot afford more.
body:
India's poorest households just lost more than half their subsidised cooking gas allocation. The Centre has quietly reduced the number of LPG cylinders eligible for the ₹300 subsidy under the Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana from nine per year to four — a cut that affects roughly 10 crore women who were given free gas connections under the flagship welfare scheme.

The government's defence is mathematical, and technically accurate. The average Ujjwala household consumes approximately four refills a year. Subsidising nine cylinders, the argument goes, meant padding the entitlement far beyond actual usage. A petroleum ministry official told reporters that the subsidy is now calibrated to "broadly match the average annual consumption of a typical Ujjwala household."

But that average is the problem. It is low precisely because millions of Ujjwala beneficiaries cannot afford to buy cylinders at full price and continue to use firewood, cow dung, and crop residue for cooking. The subsidy was designed to nudge them toward cleaner fuel. Capping it at four refills removes the ceiling that was supposed to pull consumption upward.

## The Arithmetic of the Cut

At ₹942 per cylinder (the current price in Delhi after four hikes in the past three weeks), a Ujjwala beneficiary who buys her first four cylinders in a year will pay ₹642 each — the ₹300 direct benefit transfer brings the effective cost down. Cylinder five onward, she pays the full ₹942. For a household that aspires to use LPG year-round, which requires roughly 10 to 12 cylinders, the additional five to eight unsubsidised cylinders would cost between ₹4,710 and ₹7,536.

In August 2025, the government had already trimmed the cap from 12 to nine. The latest cut, to four, completes what critics describe as a staged retreat from the scheme's founding promise: to deliver clean cooking fuel to every poor household in India.

## The Ujjwala Promise, Revisited

Launched in May 2016, the Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana was one of the Modi government's most ambitious welfare interventions. It provided deposit-free LPG connections — including the cylinder, regulator, safety hose, and a two-burner stove — to women from below-poverty-line households. By 2026, over 10.33 crore connections had been distributed.

The programme was hailed internationally as a public health breakthrough. Household air pollution from solid fuel cooking kills an estimated 600,000 Indians annually, according to WHO data. Ujjwala offered a direct pathway out of that crisis.

But the refill numbers always told a more complicated story. Many beneficiaries took the free connection but could not afford regular refills, especially after global crude prices began climbing. The average consumption of 3.87 refills per year — the number the government cites to justify the cap — is itself a symptom of affordability failure, not a sign that four cylinders are sufficient.

## What NRI Families Should Know

For diaspora households sending remittances to parents and relatives in rural India, the subsidy cut means a direct increase in household expenses. An elderly mother in a village in Madhya Pradesh or Jharkhand who was already struggling to afford nine cylinders a year will now receive government support for fewer than half of them.

The broader concern is policy direction. Oil marketing companies are currently absorbing under-recoveries of approximately ₹700 per domestic LPG cylinder — the gap between the market-linked price and what consumers actually pay. The ₹30,000 crore compensation approved by the Cabinet only partly offsets these losses. If global crude stays above $90, further price hikes and subsidy tightening are likely.

The ₹29 hike announced last week, the petroleum ministry said, works out to "₹1 per day and 20 paisa per day per household member." That framing is designed to minimise. For a household earning ₹8,000 a month, cooking fuel that costs ₹942 per cylinder is not a rounding error. It is a decision between food and fire.

*Sources: Times of India, Indian Economic Observer, The S Bharat, Press Information Bureau*
